beats: Hook: why did GPU programmers stop thinking about threads and start thinking about tiles? Shouting orders at every single cook (line_tiles_megaphone) vs handing a team one tray (line_tiles_tray_handoff).
The curse of specialization: tensor cores, TMA, warp specialization and new tricks like software pipelining arrive faster than automatic compilers grow primitives (line_tiles_gadget_pile).

The performance-productivity map: PTX/CUDA = cooking everything from scratch (line_tiles_scratch_cook), TVM = an automatic bread machine (line_tiles_bread_machine), PyTorch = press one button (line_tiles_microwave), and the gap DSLs fill: the meal kit (line_tiles_meal_kit).
Triton (Tillet et al. 2019): program the block, not the thread; each block takes one tile of the output (line_tiles_sheet_cake).
What the compiler does inside the block: pipelining and prefetching, TMA brings whole tiles (line_tiles_prefetch_line).

Who specifies what: CUDA: memory, threads, tensor cores, vectors all by hand; Triton: tiles by hand, the rest automatic; TVM: all automatic, fair speed (reuse the four cooking drawings as column heads).
Today: lower than Triton for more control (Gluon, TileLang, TLX), higher for less code (Helion), distributed (Triton-Distributed, ParallelKitten) (line_tiles_staircase, line_knob_board).
Takeaway: the tile is the sweet spot between control and convenience; 'still a long way to go'; L15 continues the story.
Cover (line_cover_l09_04; for the X post and thumbnails, not a film beat): a student programmer hands a team of line cooks one tray cut into equal squares instead of ordering each cook.
